76. DI Lifetimes

○
Simple picture

Transient means a new cup each request for the service, scoped means one cup per web request, and singleton means one shared tank for the app.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

A scoped service instance is reused within one request scope; singleton instances must be thread-safe and cannot directly depend on shorter-lived services. DbContext is scoped by default.

Watch for this

A singleton holding request/user state leaks across users. Capturing a scoped service inside a singleton creates a captive dependency.

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain DI Lifetimes, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

Memorise this table:

LifetimeMeaningTypical use
Transientnew instance each resolutionlightweight stateless helper
Scopedone instance per HTTP requestapplication service, EF DbContext
Singletonone instance for app lifetimeshared thread-safe long-lived service

Code:

csharp
builder.Services.AddTransient<IClock, Clock>();

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();

builder.Services.AddSingleton<ICacheStats, CacheStats>();

Interview trap

Do not casually inject a scoped service into a singleton.

A singleton lives much longer than a request-scoped dependency.

A stateless sender can be transient unless its underlying client is deliberately shared. A singleton must not capture a scoped dependency, or request state can escape its scope.

77. Inversion of Control

○
Simple picture

Inversion of Control means the application framework calls and assembles your code, instead of each object controlling construction itself.

Technical truth

        ↓
container gives dependency
        ↓
OrderService uses it

89. S — Single Responsibility Principle

○
Simple picture

Single Responsibility means one module should have one coherent reason to change, not merely one method.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

Group behaviour around an actor or policy boundary. Order pricing, persistence and notification change for different reasons and should not be tangled.

Watch for this

Splitting every five lines into a new class creates ceremony without cohesion. SRP is about change forces.

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain S — Single Responsibility Principle, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

“

A component should have one primary reason to change.

Bad:

text
OrderService
- calculate totals
- query DB
- send email
- generate PDF
- process Stripe
- write logs

Better responsibilities:

text
OrderService
PaymentService
EmailService
OrderRepository
InvoiceGenerator

Do not interpret SRP as “every class must have one tiny method”.

Think:

“

Keep unrelated reasons for change separate.

90. O — Open/Closed

○
Simple picture

Open/Closed means add a new plug-in behaviour without reopening stable working code for every variation.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

Polymorphism, composition and data-driven policies can create extension points. Apply them where variation is expected and costly, not everywhere pre-emptively.

Watch for this

A switch is not automatically a violation. For a small closed set, it may be clearer than an abstraction.

   ↑
StripePaymentService
PayPalPaymentService
AdyenPaymentService

New implementation can be added behind the abstraction.

91. L — Liskov Substitution

○
Simple picture

Liskov says a replacement must keep the promises callers rely on.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

A subtype must preserve valid inputs, expected outputs, invariants and observable behaviour of its base abstraction. Contract compatibility matters more than class shape.

Watch for this

Inheritance that throws NotSupportedException for normal base operations is a warning that the ‘is-a’ claim is false.

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain L — Liskov Substitution, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

“

An implementation should honour the expectations of the abstraction/base type it replaces.

If code expects:

text
IPaymentService.PayAsync

an implementation should not violate the conceptual contract in surprising ways.

92. I — Interface Segregation

○
Simple picture

Interface Segregation means give each client a small remote control with only the buttons it needs.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

Split contracts by cohesive client capabilities so implementations and callers do not depend on unrelated members.

Watch for this

One-method interfaces are not automatically good. Split along usage and change boundaries, not arbitrary size.

{

    void Email();
    void Print();
    void DeleteDatabase();
}

Prefer smaller focused contracts.

93. D — Dependency Inversion

○
Simple picture

Dependency Inversion says important policy should depend on stable promises, while replaceable details implement those promises.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

High-level application code owns or consumes abstractions; database, email and payment adapters sit outside. DI wires the direction at runtime.

Watch for this

Putting an interface in the infrastructure project while the core depends on that project may preserve DI syntax but violate architectural direction.

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain D — Dependency Inversion, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

High-level policy should depend on abstractions rather than concrete low-level implementations.

Instead of:

MENTAL MODEL
OrderService → StripePaymentService

prefer:

MENTAL MODEL
OrderService → IPaymentService ← StripePaymentService

This is probably the most useful SOLID principle to connect to DI.

94. The Core Idea

○
Simple picture

Clean Architecture puts business rules in the protected centre and treats UI, database and vendors as replaceable outer tools.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

Dependencies point toward domain/application policy. Boundary models and interfaces prevent infrastructure concerns from spreading inward.

Watch for this

Do not mistake folders for architecture. If the Domain project references EF Core or ASP.NET types, the boundary is already leaking.

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain The Core Idea, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

Do not memorise folder names.

Understand the dependency direction.

MENTAL MODEL
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│ Presentation / API           │
├──────────────────────────────┤
│ Application / Use Cases      │
├──────────────────────────────┤
│ Domain / Business Rules      │
└──────────────────────────────┘
          ↑
Infrastructure implements
interfaces required by core

The business/application rules should not be tightly coupled to:

  • ASP.NET Core;
  • EF Core;
  • Stripe;
  • Redis;
  • a particular SQL database.

96. Why Do This?

○
Simple picture

Clean boundaries buy cheaper change: replacing a database or testing a rule requires touching fewer places.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

The benefit grows with system lifetime and integration volatility. The cost is additional mapping, projects and concepts, so match structure to complexity.

Watch for this

Do not sell Clean Architecture as mandatory for every CRUD app. Explain the trade-off.

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain Why Do This?, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

Benefits:

  • testability;
  • replace infrastructure;
  • clearer dependencies;
  • maintainability;
  • business logic not buried in framework code.

Trade-off:

“

More abstraction and projects can be unnecessary overhead for a tiny application.

Strong senior answer:

“

I use architectural separation where it buys maintainability; I do not create layers merely to satisfy a diagram.

97. Unit Tests

○
Simple picture

A unit test checks one small behaviour quickly with dependencies controlled at the boundary.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

Good unit tests arrange a meaningful state, act once and assert observable behaviour. They should be deterministic and independent of network, clock or database unless those are the unit.

Watch for this

Testing private methods or mirroring implementation line by line makes refactoring painful without protecting behaviour.

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain Unit Tests, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

Test one piece of logic in isolation.

Example:

csharp
public class PricingService
{
    public decimal ApplyDiscount(
        decimal total,
        decimal discountPercentage)
    {
        return total -
            (total * discountPercentage / 100m);
    }
}

xUnit style:

csharp
[Fact]
public void ApplyDiscount_ReturnsDiscountedPrice()
{
    // Arrange
    var service = new PricingService();

    // Act
    decimal result =
        service.ApplyDiscount(100m, 10m);

    // Assert
    Assert.Equal(90m, result);
}

Memorise:

text
Arrange
Act
Assert

○
Simple picture

Technical truth

Over-mocking produces tests that pass even when real components cannot integrate and couples tests to internal call order.

Good candidates:

  • payment provider;
  • external HTTP API;
  • repository;
  • clock/time;
  • email provider.

Do not mock every internal class just because a mocking library exists.

102. Difference

○
Simple picture

Authentication asks ‘who are you?’; authorization asks ‘may that identity perform this action on this resource?’

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

ASP.NET Core authentication builds a ClaimsPrincipal; authorization evaluates roles, claims, policies and sometimes resource-specific rules. Both belong before sensitive business action.

Watch for this

A valid token is not permission. Hiding a button is not enforcement; the API must authorise every protected operation.

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain Difference, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

Memorise:

text
Authentication
=
Who are you?

Authorization
=
Are you allowed to do this?

For APIs:

MENTAL MODEL
JWT/token
   ↓
authentication
   ↓
identity established
   ↓
authorization policy/role
   ↓
endpoint allowed or denied

Common trap:

text
401 = authentication problem
403 = authenticated but forbidden

104. Metrics vs Logs vs Traces

○
Simple picture

Logs tell stories, metrics show numerical trends, and traces follow one request across components.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

Metrics support alerting and capacity signals; traces connect distributed spans; logs explain discrete context. Correlation identifiers tie the three views together.

Watch for this

Collecting telemetry without service-level questions creates cost rather than observability. High-cardinality labels can overwhelm metric systems.

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain Metrics vs Logs vs Traces, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

Simple mental model:

MENTAL MODEL
Logs
→ what happened?

Metrics
→ how much/how often/how fast?

Traces
→ where did one request spend its time?

For diagnosing a slow API, you want all three.

105. Slow Endpoint Interview Answer

○
Simple picture

A slow endpoint is a detective case: reproduce, measure, locate the expensive span, change one cause and verify.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

Start with latency percentiles and traces, then inspect SQL/query plans, dependency time, payload size, allocation/CPU and resource saturation. Compare before and after under representative load.

Watch for this

Do not jump straight to caching. It can hide one symptom while preserving an unbounded query or downstream failure.

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain Slow Endpoint Interview Answer, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

A strong response:

“

I would measure before optimising. I’d inspect metrics, logs and traces to determine whether latency is in the database, external calls, CPU, allocation/GC, connection pools, locks, or synchronous blocking. For EF Core I’d look for N+1 queries, missing indexes, loading too much data, unnecessary tracking, and excessive round trips. Then I’d optimise the measured bottleneck, perhaps changing the query, adding caching, moving non-critical work to a queue, or scaling the relevant resource.

109. Stateless Services

○
Simple picture

A stateless API does not keep a user's essential conversation only inside one server's memory.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

Any healthy instance can handle the next request because durable state lives in databases, caches or tokens with appropriate consistency and security.

Watch for this

Stateless does not mean ‘no state anywhere.’ Local caches and connection pools exist, but correctness cannot depend on one instance.

Prove you understand

110. Load Balancer

○
Simple picture

A load balancer is a traffic officer distributing requests among healthy service instances.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

It may terminate TLS, run health checks and use round-robin, least-connections or other strategies. Retry and connection behaviour affect perceived balancing.

Watch for this

A load balancer cannot make an unhealthy dependency healthy. Sticky sessions can weaken resilience and scaling flexibility.

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain Load Balancer, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

MENTAL MODEL
                  ┌── API 1
Client → Load Balancer ── API 2
                  └── API 3

Responsibilities can include:

  • distribute traffic;
  • avoid unhealthy instances;
  • TLS termination;
  • routing.

Interview phrase:

“

A load balancer distributes requests across healthy application instances to improve utilisation, availability, and horizontal scalability.

111. Health Checks

○
Simple picture

A health check is a small diagnostic answering whether an instance is alive and whether it is ready for traffic.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

Liveness should detect a wedged process; readiness should reflect whether the instance can serve. Dependency checks need timeouts and must avoid causing overload.

Watch for this

Marking an instance unhealthy whenever a shared database blips can remove every instance at once. Design degraded behaviour thoughtfully.

/API-2 → unhealthy
/API-3 → healthy

Traffic:

text
API-1 ✓
API-2 ✗
API-3 ✓

You may distinguish:

liveness  → process alive?
readiness → ready to receive traffic?

112. Database Bottleneck

○
Simple picture

The database often becomes the narrowest doorway because every scaled API still queues at shared storage.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

Measure slow queries, locks, connection pools, I/O and CPU. Improve indexes and query shape, reduce unnecessary round trips, then consider replicas, partitioning or architectural change.

Watch for this

Scaling the web tier first can increase database pressure. Denormalisation and sharding are later tools with consistency costs.

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain Database Bottleneck, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

Adding API instances does not automatically scale the database.

MENTAL MODEL
API 1 ─┐
API 2 ─┼──→ ONE database
API 3 ─┤
API 4 ─┘

Potential bottlenecks:

  • slow queries;
  • indexes;
  • connection limits;
  • lock contention;
  • hot rows;
  • huge result sets.

Always ask:

“

Where is the real bottleneck?

113. Caching

○
Simple picture

A cache keeps suitable reused answers closer so expensive work need not be repeated every time.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

Cache-aside loads on miss and stores with an expiry. Key design, TTL, invalidation, stampede control and consistency determine correctness.

Watch for this

Never cache merely because reads are slow. Sensitive, user-specific or rapidly changing data needs careful scope and invalidation.

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain Caching, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

Basic:

MENTAL MODEL
API
 ├──→ Cache
 └──→ Database

Cache-aside mental model:

text
1. check cache
2. hit? return
3. miss? read DB
4. store result in cache
5. return

Benefits:

  • lower latency;
  • fewer database reads.

Trade-offs:

  • stale data;
  • invalidation;
  • consistency;
  • memory.

Great interview sentence:

“

Caching trades freshness and complexity for lower latency and reduced backend load.

114. Message Queues

○
Simple picture

A queue is a durable waiting line that separates accepting work from completing slower background work.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

Producers publish messages; consumers process independently with acknowledgements, retries and dead-letter handling. This smooths spikes and reduces temporal coupling.

Watch for this

Delivery is commonly at least once, so consumers must handle duplicates. A queued action is not immediately complete from the user's perspective.

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain Message Queues, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

Some work does not need to complete inside the HTTP request.

Bad:

MENTAL MODEL
POST order
  ↓
charge
  ↓
save
  ↓
generate invoice
  ↓
send email
  ↓
call analytics
  ↓
wait

Better for suitable asynchronous work:

MENTAL MODEL
POST order
  ↓
API
  ↓
save order
  ↓
publish message
  ↓
return response

Queue
  ↓
Worker
  ↓
email / invoice / analytics

Benefits:

  • decoupling;
  • buffering;
  • absorb spikes;
  • retries.

Important interview words:

text
idempotency
retry
dead-letter queue
eventual consistency

115. Idempotency

○
Simple picture

Idempotency means repeating the same request has the same intended effect as processing it once.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

Use a client-supplied key, store the result/operation state atomically and return the prior outcome for duplicates within a defined scope and retention period.

Watch for this

A unique key check followed by a separate write can race. Idempotency needs an atomic boundary and a clear definition of ‘same request.’

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain Idempotency, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

If a message is delivered twice:

text
charge customer twice?

Bad.

An idempotent consumer ensures retrying the same operation does not create unintended duplicate effects.

Examples:

text
idempotency key
processed-message table
unique operation ID

116. Monolith vs Microservices

○
Simple picture

A monolith is one deployable building; microservices are separate buildings connected by roads.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

A modular monolith keeps in-process transactions and simpler operations while enforcing internal boundaries. Microservices add independent deployment/scale but introduce networks, distributed data and observability burden.

Watch for this

Splitting by technical layers creates distributed coupling. Service boundaries should follow business capabilities and team ownership.

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain Monolith vs Microservices, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

Do not say:

“

Microservices are better because they scale.

Better:

Modular monolith

Advantages:

  • simpler deployment;
  • simpler debugging;
  • easier transactions;
  • fewer distributed failure modes.

Microservices

Potential advantages:

  • independent deployment;
  • independent scaling;
  • team/domain autonomy.

Costs:

  • network failure;
  • eventual consistency;
  • tracing;
  • deployment complexity;
  • data ownership;
  • message reliability;
  • operational overhead.

Strong answer:

“

I would normally start with the simplest architecture that satisfies the requirements. I’d move toward independently deployable services when there are real domain, team, release, or scaling boundaries that justify the distributed-system cost.

117. Resilience

○
Simple picture

Resilience is designing the system to bend when dependencies are slow or unavailable instead of collapsing everywhere.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

Use timeouts, bounded retries with jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads, rate limits and fallbacks according to failure semantics and idempotency.

Watch for this

Retries multiply load during outages. Never retry indefinitely or retry non-idempotent work without safeguards.

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain Resilience, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

External services fail.

Think:

text
timeout
retry
circuit breaker
fallback
bulkhead

Important nuance:

“

Retries are not automatically safe. Retrying a non-idempotent operation such as a payment can create duplicates unless the operation supports idempotency.

119. Security Checklist

○
Simple picture

Security is a set of locked boundaries: validate input, minimise authority, protect secrets and record important actions.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

Use TLS, secure authentication, resource-level authorization, parameterised data access, secret stores, dependency patching, rate limits and safe error responses as layered controls.

Watch for this

Do not invent crypto, trust client claims or expose stack traces. Security is a continuing design and operations responsibility.

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain Security Checklist, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

For a Web API, remember:

text
authentication
authorization
HTTPS
input validation

How to explain:

  1. Start simple.

  3. Add horizontal instances if load requires it.
  4. Load balancer routes only to healthy instances.

  6. Cache only proven read-heavy data.
  7. Move non-critical asynchronous work to queue.
  8. Add observability.
  9. Test under realistic load.
  10. Scale the measured bottleneck.

src/OrderFlow.Application/OrderAlgorithms.cs
namespace OrderFlow.Application;

public static class OrderAlgorithms
{
    public static (int First, int Second)? FindPairWithTargetTotal(
        IReadOnlyList<decimal> totals,
        decimal target)
    {
        var seen = new Dictionary<decimal, int>();

        for (var index = 0; index < totals.Count; index++)
        {
            var needed = target - totals[index];
            if (seen.TryGetValue(needed, out var otherIndex))
                return (otherIndex, index);

            seen[totals[index]] = index;
        }

        return null;
    }

    public static int BinarySearch(IReadOnlyList<int> sortedOrderNumbers, int target)
    {
        var left = 0;
        var right = sortedOrderNumbers.Count - 1;

        while (left <= right)
        {
            var middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
            if (sortedOrderNumbers[middle] == target)
                return middle;

            if (sortedOrderNumbers[middle] < target)
                left = middle + 1;
            else
                right = middle - 1;
        }

        return -1;
    }

    public static bool ContainsDuplicateOrderNumber(IEnumerable<int> orderNumbers)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(orderNumbers);

        var seen = new HashSet<int>();

        foreach (var number in orderNumbers)
        {
            if (!seen.Add(number))
                return true;
        }

        return false;
    }

    public static bool IsPalindromeOrderReference(string value)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(value);

        var normalised = new string(value
            .Where(char.IsLetterOrDigit)
            .Select(char.ToUpperInvariant)
            .ToArray());

        for (var left = 0; left < normalised.Length / 2; left++)
        {
            if (normalised[left] != normalised[normalised.Length - 1 - left])
                return false;
        }

        return true;
    }

    public static bool HasBalancedGrouping(string value)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(value);

        var expected = new Stack<char>();

        foreach (var character in value)
        {
            if (character == '(')
                expected.Push(')');
            else if (character == '[')
                expected.Push(']');
            else if (character == '{')
                expected.Push('}');
            else if (character is ')' or ']' or '}')
            {
                if (expected.Count == 0 || expected.Pop() != character)
                    return false;
            }
        }

        return expected.Count == 0;
    }

    public static decimal HighestWindowTotal(IReadOnlyList<decimal> totals, int windowSize)
    {
        ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(totals);

        if (windowSize <= 0 || windowSize > totals.Count)
            throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(windowSize));

        var current = totals.Take(windowSize).Sum();
        var best = current;

        for (var right = windowSize; right < totals.Count; right++)
        {
            current += totals[right] - totals[right - windowSize];
            best = Math.Max(best, current);
        }

        return best;
    }
}
tests/OrderFlow.UnitTests/OrderAlgorithmsTests.cs
using OrderFlow.Application;

namespace OrderFlow.UnitTests;

public sealed class OrderAlgorithmsTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Pair_search_returns_two_different_matching_positions()
    {
        var match = OrderAlgorithms.FindPairWithTargetTotal([20m, 35m, 80m, 65m], 100m);

        Assert.Equal((0, 2), match);
    }

    [Theory]
    [InlineData(10, 0)]
    [InlineData(30, 2)]
    [InlineData(50, 4)]
    [InlineData(99, -1)]
    public void Binary_search_finds_edges_middle_or_missing(int target, int expected)
    {
        Assert.Equal(expected, OrderAlgorithms.BinarySearch([10, 20, 30, 40, 50], target));
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Duplicate_detection_handles_empty_unique_and_repeated_numbers()
    {
        Assert.False(OrderAlgorithms.ContainsDuplicateOrderNumber([]));
        Assert.False(OrderAlgorithms.ContainsDuplicateOrderNumber([101, 102, 103]));
        Assert.True(OrderAlgorithms.ContainsDuplicateOrderNumber([101, 102, 101]));
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Duplicate_detection_rejects_a_null_sequence()
    {
        Assert.Throws<ArgumentNullException>(() => OrderAlgorithms.ContainsDuplicateOrderNumber(null!));
    }

    [Theory]
    [InlineData("OF-11-FO", true)]
    [InlineData("Never odd or even", true)]
    [InlineData("OF-1234", false)]
    public void Palindrome_check_normalises_case_and_punctuation(string value, bool expected)
    {
        Assert.Equal(expected, OrderAlgorithms.IsPalindromeOrderReference(value));
    }

    [Theory]
    [InlineData("({[]})", true)]
    [InlineData("([)]", false)]
    [InlineData("(()", false)]
    [InlineData("order-{reference}", true)]
    public void Grouping_validation_detects_wrong_order_and_unfinished_pairs(string value, bool expected)
    {
        Assert.Equal(expected, OrderAlgorithms.HasBalancedGrouping(value));
    }

    [Fact]
    public void Sliding_window_returns_the_largest_consecutive_total()
    {
        Assert.Equal(16m, OrderAlgorithms.HighestWindowTotal([4m, 8m, 2m, 10m, 6m], 2));
        Assert.Equal(30m, OrderAlgorithms.HighestWindowTotal([4m, 8m, 2m, 10m, 6m], 5));
    }

    [Theory]
    [InlineData(0)]
    [InlineData(4)]
    public void Sliding_window_rejects_an_invalid_window_size(int windowSize)
    {
        Assert.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>(() =>
            OrderAlgorithms.HighestWindowTotal([1m, 2m, 3m], windowSize));
    }
}

123. Two Sum

○
Simple picture

Two Sum remembers numbers already seen so each new number can ask whether its missing partner exists.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

For each value x, compute target - x, check the dictionary, then store x and its index. This gives O(n) expected time and O(n) space.

Watch for this

Check before inserting when the same element cannot be reused. Decide what duplicate values and ‘no solution’ should return.

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain Two Sum, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

Problem:

“

Return indexes of two numbers adding to target.

Brute force:

text
every i
  every j

Usually:

text
O(n²)

Better:

csharp
public static int[] TwoSum(
    int[] nums,
    int target)
{
    var seen =
        new Dictionary<int, int>();

    for (int i = 0;
         i < nums.Length;
         i++)
    {
        int needed =
            target - nums[i];

        if (seen.TryGetValue(
                needed,
                out int previousIndex))
        {
            return
            [
                previousIndex,
                i
            ];
        }

        seen[nums[i]] = i;
    }

    return [];
}

Reason aloud:

“

For each number I need to know whether its complement has already appeared. A dictionary gives average O(1) lookup, reducing the overall scan to O(n) time with O(n) extra space.

○
Simple picture

Two pointers place one reader at each end and move inward while the compared characters agree.

Technical truth

csharp
public static bool IsPalindrome(
    string text)
{
    int left = 0;
    int right = text.Length - 1;

    while (left < right)
    {
        if (text[left] != text[right])
        {
            return false;
        }

        left++;
        right--;
    }

    return true;
}

public static bool IsPalindromeOrderReference(string value)
{
    ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(value);
    var normalised = new string(value.Where(char.IsLetterOrDigit)
        .Select(char.ToUpperInvariant).ToArray());
    for (var left = 0; left < normalised.Length / 2; left++)
        if (normalised[left] != normalised[normalised.Length - 1 - left]) return false;
    return true;
}

126. Valid Parentheses — Stack

○
Simple picture

Valid Parentheses uses a stack like open boxes: every closing bracket must match the most recently opened box.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

Push opening delimiters; for a closing delimiter, require a non-empty stack and matching top; valid input ends with an empty stack. O(n) time, O(n) worst-case space.

Watch for this

Checking only bracket counts misses incorrect nesting such as ([)].

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain Valid Parentheses — Stack, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

csharp
public static bool IsValid(
    string input)
{
    Stack<char> stack = new();

    foreach (char c in input)
    {
        if (c is '(' or '[' or '{')
        {
            stack.Push(c);
            continue;
        }

        if (stack.Count == 0)
        {
            return false;
        }

        char open = stack.Pop();

        if (
            (c == ')' && open != '(') ||
            (c == ']' && open != '[') ||
            (c == '}' && open != '{')
        )
        {
            return false;
        }
    }

    return stack.Count == 0;
}

Why stack?

text
last opened
=
first that must close

public static bool HasBalancedGrouping(string value)
{
    ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(value);
    var expected = new Stack<char>();
    foreach (var character in value)
    {
        if (character == '(') expected.Push(')');
        else if (character == '[') expected.Push(']');
        else if (character == '{') expected.Push('}');
        else if ((character is ')' or ']' or '}') &&
                 (expected.Count == 0 || expected.Pop() != character)) return false;
    }
    return expected.Count == 0;
}

127. Binary Search

○
Simple picture

Binary search repeatedly discards the half that cannot contain the answer.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

Maintain an inclusive or half-open invariant, compute the midpoint safely and update bounds without retaining the midpoint. It requires sorted or monotonic search space and takes O(log n) comparisons.

Watch for this

Most bugs are boundary-contract bugs. Say what left and right mean before writing the loop.

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain Binary Search, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

Requires sorted input.

csharp
public static int BinarySearch(
    int[] nums,
    int target)
{
    int left = 0;
    int right = nums.Length - 1;

    while (left <= right)
    {
        int middle =
            left + (right - left) / 2;

        if (nums[middle] == target)
        {
            return middle;
        }

        if (nums[middle] < target)
        {
            left = middle + 1;
        }
        else
        {
            right = middle - 1;
        }
    }

    return -1;
}

Complexity:

text
O(log n)

because you discard roughly half the remaining search space each step.

public static int BinarySearch(IReadOnlyList<int> sortedOrderNumbers, int target)
{
    var left = 0;
    var right = sortedOrderNumbers.Count - 1;
    while (left <= right)
    {
        var middle = left + (right - left) / 2;
        if (sortedOrderNumbers[middle] == target) return middle;
        if (sortedOrderNumbers[middle] < target) left = middle + 1;
        else right = middle - 1;
    }
    return -1;
}

128. Sliding Window

○
Simple picture

A sliding window maintains facts about one moving contiguous range instead of recalculating every range from scratch.

Go one layer deepertechnical truth · trap · recall check
Technical truth

Expand the right edge, update state, shrink the left edge while constraints fail, and record the best valid window. Many problems become O(n) because each item enters and leaves once.

Watch for this

Use it only when the target is contiguous and the window condition can be maintained incrementally.

Prove you understand

Without looking: explain Sliding Window, point to where it belongs in OrderFlow, then name one mistake or trade-off.

Problem:

“

Maximum sum of any k consecutive values.

csharp
public static int MaxWindowSum(
    int[] nums,
    int k)
{
    int sum = 0;

    for (int i = 0;
         i < k;
         i++)
    {
        sum += nums[i];
    }

    int best = sum;

    for (int right = k;
         right < nums.Length;
         right++)
    {
        sum += nums[right];
        sum -= nums[right - k];

        best = Math.Max(
            best,
            sum
        );
    }

    return best;
}

src/OrderFlow.Application/OrderAlgorithms.cs · csharp
public static decimal HighestWindowTotal(IReadOnlyList<decimal> totals, int windowSize)
{
    ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(totals);
    if (windowSize <= 0 || windowSize > totals.Count) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(windowSize));
    var current = totals.Take(windowSize).Sum();
    var best = current;
    for (var right = windowSize; right < totals.Count; right++)
    {
        current += totals[right] - totals[right - windowSize];
        best = Math.Max(best, current);
    }
    return best;
}

Final Message to Yourself

You are not trying to become a new developer overnight.

You are rebuilding access to knowledge you have already used.

The interview target is not:

“

“I know every method in .NET.”

It is:

“

“I understand the mainstream C#/.NET concepts, I can write normal C# again, I understand how an ASP.NET Core request flows through the application, I can explain DI/EF Core/architecture/testing/scaling, and I can reason through a simple coding problem.”

That is a realistic target for this crash session.
